description_full: Cullen/Frost Bankers, Inc. operates as the bank holding company for Frost Bank that provides commercial and consumer banking services in Texas. The company offers commercial banking services to corporations, including financing for industrial and commercial properties, interim construction related to industrial and commercial properties, equipment, inventories and accounts receivables, and acquisitions; and treasury management services. It also provides consumer banking services, such as checking accounts, automated-teller machines (ATMs), overdraft facilities, installment and real estate loans, first mortgage loans, home equity loans and lines of credit, drive-in and night deposit services, safe deposit facilities, and brokerage services. In addition, the company offers international banking services comprising deposits, loans, letters of credit, foreign collections, funds transmitting, and foreign exchange services; correspondent banking activities, including check clearing, transfer of funds, fixed income security services, and securities custody and clearance services. Further, it offers trust, investment, agency, and custodial services for individual and corporate clients; capital market services that include sales and trading, new issue underwriting, money market trading, advisory, and securities safekeeping and clearance; and support for international business activities, including foreign exchange, letters of credit, export-import financing, and other related activities. Additionally, the company offers insurance and securities brokerage services; holding of securities for investment purposes; and investment management services for mutual funds, institutions, and individuals. It serves energy, manufacturing, services, construction, retail, telecommunications, healthcare, military, and transportation industries. Cullen/Frost Bankers, Inc. was founded in 1868 and is headquartered in San Antonio, Texas.

financial_summary: Cullen/Frost Bankers, Inc. is a mid-cap financial services business with a $9.7B market cap on $2.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $127M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.42×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA.
Shareholder yield of 4.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.2% of the shares.

Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 27% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.00 vs 5y 0.70), so read it loosely.
About $73.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $75.82 (margin of safety -105%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 17%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $53.57 to $108 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 75.8 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 13% above its 10-year median.
The 14 covering analysts target $173 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 18.0% annual cash-flow growth, 13pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.24).
It converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 3.62% and an efficiency ratio of 62%.
It earns a 14% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 14.4% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 0.55% of the book, a clean credit profile.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.6% over 3 years, 9.2% over 5 years and 7.7% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 9% of profits supports about 1.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 6.7% on average.
Analysts expect 9.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 6.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 96%.
It returns 4.3% a year to shareholders (1.6% in buybacks and 2.7% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 32 consecutive years, raising it 7.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,008 employees, each generates about $372K of revenue, 0.7x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 6.7% a year.
That works out to $21K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
